title: One Value, One Owner
goal: The rule behind this whole deck: every value has exactly one owner.

sections.text: Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. When you assign a value to a new variable, or pass it to a function by value, ownership moves. The old variable becomes invalid, and the compiler rejects any later use of it. This is error `E0382`, and you will meet it often in this deck.

sections.caption: A move invalidates the old variable.

sections.text: If you only need to read a value, you do not need to own it. A reference, written `&name`, borrows the value. The owner keeps it, and the borrow ends when it is no longer used. Borrowing is the default way to pass data to a function that only reads it.

sections.caption: A borrow leaves ownership where it was.

sections.text: Some types opt out of moving. Simple types like `i32`, `bool`, and `char` implement the `Copy` trait. Passing them duplicates the value bit for bit, and the original stays valid. Types that own heap memory, like `String` and `Vec`, are not `Copy`, because duplicating them would need an allocation.
The puzzles in this deck train one decision: read the code, decide whether each value should move, be borrowed, or be copied, and pay nothing extra.

explanation: Every value has one owner. Borrow to read, move to transfer, and Copy types duplicate for free.
